name: Bystander Effect
description: The more people who seem to be present, the less personally responsible any one person may feel to help. Visible others can shift a situation from 'I should act' to 'someone else probably will.'
design_relevance_note: Relevant to abuse reporting, escalation flows, group chats, incident response, community safety, collaborative tools, and help-request UX where a request sent to 'everyone' can end up owned by no one.
prevalence_note: Common in trust-and-safety, moderation, and community-design work; the term is not as universal in generic interface design, but it is a standard reference whenever products depend on users intervening or reporting harm.

findings.description: A fixed-effects meta-analysis of 105 independent effect sizes (>7,700 participants, 1960s-2010 literature) confirmed an overall bystander effect of g = -0.35 (more bystanders present, less individual helping), but found the effect is significantly attenuated — sometimes reversing to non-negative — when the emergency is perceived as genuinely dangerous (vs. non-dangerous), when a perpetrator is present, and when the cost of intervening is physical rather than non-physical; bystanders can also function as a source of welcome physical support rather than diffusion of responsibility under specific conditions (e.g., all-male groups, non-stranger bystanders).
findings.source_title: The bystander-effect: A meta-analytic review on bystander intervention in dangerous and non-dangerous emergencies

findings.description: Participants who believed they were the sole witness to a staged emergency (an apparent epileptic seizure overheard via intercom) reported it faster and more often than participants who believed 1 or 4 other unseen bystanders also witnessed it (p < .01) — the presence of other perceived bystanders reduced individual felt responsibility to act, independent of participant sex or personality/background measures, which were not predictive of helping.
findings.source_title: Bystander intervention in emergencies: Diffusion of responsibility
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

applications.title: A proposed Amber Alert redesign showing a recipient's personal proximity to a missing child
applications.description: A redesign concept for Amber Alert notifications proposes showing a live map of the recipient's own location relative to a missing child and suspect's last-known area, intended to counteract the bystander effect by making the emergency feel personally relevant rather than something 'someone else nearby' will handle.
applications.ethical_note: A genuinely public-interest application with no commercial or engagement motive -- even as an unimplemented concept, it's worth including as this corpus's first hypothetical_teaching_example, illustrating that provenance grading applies honestly in both directions: not just downgrading suspicious claims, but correctly labeling a well-intentioned idea as unimplemented rather than overstating it as real.

applications.title: Raymond Zack's 2011 drowning: firefighters, police, and bystanders each waited for someone else to act
applications.description: In 2011, Raymond Zack stood in shallow ocean water off Alameda, California for nearly an hour before drowning while firefighters, police officers, and dozens of bystanders watched -- firefighters expected police to act, police expected firefighters to act, and a bystander who attempted a rescue was told by officials to stand down because 'the authorities would take care of it.'
applications.ethical_note: A fatal real-world illustration of the bystander effect at an institutional scale (professional responders, not just civilian onlookers, deferred to one another) -- distinct from this graph's existing AmberAlert design example; directly relevant to any multi-party product workflow (support tickets, moderation queues, shared inboxes) where an action is 'someone else's job' until explicitly assigned to a specific owner.
